scenario: A landlord's tenant Pemberton has moved out and left the unit a mess, still owing past-due rent, with a $2,800 deposit on hand. The biggest problem is that a complete worked-out answer file sits in the assistant's own input folder: it spells out the property name, unit, address, the rent balance, prices, market rent, the full task list, the urgent sign-off header, and even pre-written contractor texts, so any assistant that simply lists its input files is handed the entire answer it was supposed to figure out from the photos and data. On top of that, several criteria are wrong. One penalizes the assistant for asking the user to confirm the past-due balance, but that balance is never actually provided anywhere, so the honest and correct thing to do is to ask, and this criterion punishes that correct behavior. Another requires logging the portfolio debt as a specific figure that appears in no input, is not derivable, and is even contradicted by the answer file's own numbers, so it rewards a wrong value. A third rigidly demands exactly eight repair tasks when the prompt never states a count, so a correct response that itemizes the same real damage at a slightly different level of detail is rejected. A fourth criterion is just the mirror image of another one, both judging the single question of whether the real property details were used, which is redundant and is counted once. A separate concern about the unit tests was dropped: the two failing tests cited do not actually exist in the real test file, and grading the real file shows only one over-strict test, which is not enough to fail on the tests alone. Two other criteria that pin a specific risk label and a specific balance are set aside because those exact values cannot be confirmed from the prompt.
fix: Remove the complete worked-solution audit file from the input folder so the answer is not handed to the assistant. Rewrite the balance criterion so it does not penalize asking the user to confirm a value that is never stated; reward confirming the genuinely-missing balance instead. Replace the fixed portfolio-debt figure with the real debt supported by the inputs (or make it accept any correctly-derived total). Drop the rigid 'eight tasks' count and instead reward itemizing the actual repair, cleaning, and renovation work at a reasonable level of detail. Merge the two mirror-image property-detail criteria into a single check. Fix or remove the test that demands the exact literal urgent header so a correct alternative wording is not failed.

Remove the fabricated 'Sapphire Preferred' product name from both credit-card criteria and accept the card identified simply as the Chase card with the correct balance. Loosen the memory-location criterion so any reasonable memory file location is accepted rather than requiring the workspace root.

One photo shows pappardelle in a creamy tomato sauce with a few matte dark-red discs that read equally well as sun-dried tomato or as chorizo, and the assistant's own image tool called it ambiguous and leaned toward meat-free. Instead, accept either defensible classification of that photo and check that the plan's length and meatless target follow correctly from whichever count the response chose (length in weeks equal to the meatless meals, meatless target equal to double the meat meals). Alternatively, replace the ambiguous photo with one whose contents are clearly meat or clearly meatless so the intended counts are unambiguous.

scenario: A parent is assembling their 11-year-old daughter's science-fair project for her portfolio and has uploaded her typed write-up, her original notes, display-board photos, and fair-night pictures, noting that she wrote it from memory so some details may be off. scenario: Rebecca ran a 5K and is deciding whether to commit to a 10K in October, so she uploaded photos of her handwritten training journal plus a screenshot of her Strava year stats and wants the real picture. She asks the assistant to go through every journal entry, line each one up against Strava, and produce a reconciled spreadsheet, a training summary, and a fresh memory file, following the counting and 10K rules she wrote in the front of the journal.
did: A correct response had to fill in the reconciled spreadsheet one row per entry, report the true run-versus-walk counts, total mileage, running mileage, longest run, and a straight yes/no on 10K readiness under her own rule, and start a memory file recording what was done and fixed, all grounded in what the journal and Strava actually show.
why: This rubric does not fail, though it has one real defect and two small ones. The main defect: one negative criterion tries to punish the response for calling the 2/11 entry a Strava-confirmed walk, but 2/11 genuinely is a journal entry that Strava recorded as a walk, so a correct, rule-following answer gets docked for doing exactly what the rest of the rubric rewards. Two smaller issues are factual miscounts buried in criterion notes: two criteria say there were seven journal 'runs' that were really walks when the verified number is eight (the 2/3 entry is also a journal run Strava logged as a walk); because the main part of each of those criteria still grades the correct verified split, scoring is not flipped. An earlier review wanted to fail this rubric for bundling many per-date facts into single checks, for filing two checks under the wrong category, and for not naming the expected totals, but those do not hold up: listing the same kind of fact across dates is an acceptable way to check one concern, requiring the summary to report a computed value the user explicitly asked for is correct, and the category point is only advisory. None of these issues crosses the line that would fail the task.
fix: Rewrite the negative criterion so it only penalizes claiming Strava activity on the four dates that have no Strava record (2/7, 4/5, 5/28, 6/18) and remove the wrong 2/11 example. In the two criteria that mention 'seven' run-to-walk reclassifications, correct the count to eight and add the 2/3 entry to the list.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: William volunteers for a community shorebird count and needs to write up a survey he did at the Crissy Field marsh before the quarterly submission closes. He uploaded the tally card he filled out, a video clip of the bar that morning, and the survey's count protocol, and asks the assistant to follow the protocol's format, save the writeup and a matching data sheet, and only create a separate rare-bird file if something actually warrants it.

Second, the data sheet has a required column layout of species, count, and behavior, and while the species set is checked and a wrong count is guarded against, nothing checks the column layout or the behavior column content. Each of these gaps is a moderate problem, and together they push the rubric past the threshold that fails it. An earlier review instead wanted to fail it for two criteria that describe the assistant reading the Strava ride to pin down the survey date and start time, but checks that target how the assistant worked are only advisory and never fail a task, and both of those criteria are factually correct anyway.

Add a criterion that verifies the data sheet uses the exact column layout species, count, behavior, and that the behavior column is filled in.

scenario: A parent is turning their daughter Sofia's take-home folder into something usable at home before the school transition, and uploaded folder photos, a progress email, and scanned practice worksheets. They ask the assistant to work out which letters Sofia still needs to practice and capture it in a spreadsheet with named columns, then produce a short home practice plan, a parent note that keeps the teacher's exact wording, answers to the worksheet questions, and a running memory log, creating a teacher-questions file only if the marks are genuinely unreadable.
did: A correct response had to identify the letters still needing practice from the governing Letter Check page (only B, P, and Q, since D is marked as known), build the spreadsheet with the named columns, write the plan and parent note, answer the worksheets, log to memory, and skip the teacher-questions file because the marks are readable.
why: This rubric fails. The folder photos and the teacher's note make clear that the current letters to practice are B, P, and Q only: letter D carries a plain checkmark meaning it is known, the official targets come from the Letter Check page, and the note says to keep the practice table to the current target letters and that retested letters are done even if they still show on the old worksheet. Four criteria nonetheless force letter D into the answer, demanding a D row in the spreadsheet, a confused-with value and an error count for D, and a practice order of B, D, P, Q in both the spreadsheet and the plan. A correct response that lists only B, P, and Q cannot satisfy any of these four, so it gets docked for being right; four such criteria are enough on their own to fail the task. Two further moderate gaps add to it: nothing checks the decision to correctly skip the teacher-questions file, and nothing checks that the spreadsheet uses the exact required column names and order. An earlier review treated several other criteria as improperly bundled and raised two concerns drawn only from a source that is off-limits for grading, but those were set aside because listing the same kind of item is an acceptable single check and that source cannot ground a defect.
fix: Rewrite the four criteria that force letter D so they instead require the practice set and order to be B, then P, then Q, with no D target row, matching the Letter Check page and the teacher's note. Add a criterion that the teacher-questions file is correctly not created because the marks are readable. Add a criterion that the spreadsheet uses the exact column names and order: letter, status, confused_with, worksheet_error_count, practice_priority, source_note.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A pottery creator uploaded a ZIP (raw sponsor video, brief, transcript, draft captions, brand notes, and two visual references) and asked for an editor-ready package built from what is actually usable in the footage. They wanted a timestamp-based edit decision list, a cleaned caption file matching the recommended short, and thumbnail and design guidance saved to three specific files, with a final cut kept under 20 seconds and nothing overclaimed about blurry or hard-to-read moments.
did: A correct response had to inspect the actual video frame by frame, recommend a final cut under 20 seconds that keeps the sponsor mention only if the footage supports it, and save the three requested files (edit decision list, caption plan, thumbnail notes) with reasons for each major editing decision and thumbnail guidance grounded in the uploaded references without inventing unrelated products, clean logos, or a different visual style.
why: This rubric does NOT fail the task, but it has a few quality issues worth cleaning up. First, two criteria check the exact same single decision over the exact same list of items (avoiding unrelated stock photos, unrelated products, clean sponsor logos, or visual assets that were not provided), just with opposite scoring: one rewards getting it right and the other penalizes getting it wrong. That double-counts one idea, so it is treated as a single moderate issue. Second, one criterion bundles two separate requirements into one line joined by 'and': it asks both that the guidance be based on the uploaded visual references AND that it use a warm, handmade pottery look with earthy colors. A response could meet one without the other, so checking them together as a single pass/fail is a moderate issue. Third, a later criterion that asks the response to name at least two concrete elements from the references reuses the same example colors (clay, sand, charcoal) as the bundled criterion above, which is a small overlap.
